::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How to show any function from $A$ to $B$ is not onto?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4974523/how-to-show-any-function-from-a-to-b-is-not-onto), asked by [Akshhat Chaube](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1313810/akshhat-chaube) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2024-09-21; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I was reading the book A Course on Borel sets by S.M. Srivastava, and there was a theroem essentially stating the Cardinality of a set is strictly less than of it's Power set.
>
> Now in that proof we had to show that there doesn't exist any onto function from $X$ to $\mathcal P(X)$ (the power set of $X$) which will complete the proof and they did that without using anything about the Codomain being a power set
>
> My question is can we prove for a set $A$ and $B$ there doesn't exist any onto function from $A$ to $B$.
:::

In general, to show a function $f \colon A \to B$ is not surjective, it suffices to find an element $b \in B$ such that for all $a \in A$, $f(a) \neq b$.

In particular, given $f \colon X \to \mathcal{P}(X)$, let $$B = \left\{ x \in X \mid x \notin f(x) \right\}$$
Observe that $B$ is a subset of $X$, which means it's an element of $\mathcal{P}(X)$. We claim $f(x) \neq B$ for all $x \in X$.

Consider $x \in X$. Since $f(x)$ is a subset of $X$, either $x \in f(x)$ or not. Consider the cases:

1. If $x \in f(x)$, then $x \notin B$. This means $f(x) \neq B$, because one of the sets contains $x$ and the other does not.
2. If $x \notin f(x)$, then $x \in B$. This means $f(x) \neq B$, because one of the sets contains $x$ and the other does not.

Either way, we have $f(x) \neq B$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, $f$ cannot be surjective.
